t: Old Church Slavonic was shaped by Cyril and Methodius for their mission to Great Moravia from 863, with a new alphabet, Glagolitic, and translations of the Gospels and liturgy for the Christianisation of the Slavs.

Expelled from Moravia, their students carried it to Bulgaria, where Boris I founded the Preslav and Ohrid schools, Cyrillic was developed and the language became the language of state and church in 893.
As the oldest attested Slavic language it preserves features of Proto-Slavic, and as Church Slavonic it held among the eastern Slavs a place like that of Latin in Western Europe.
dyk: The full text of the Second Book of Enoch survives only in Old Church Slavonic, although the original had almost certainly been written in Greek or even Hebrew or Aramaic.
ev: Cyril and Methodius develop the Glagolitic alphabet and translate prayers and liturgical books for a mission to Great Moravia
Pope Stephen V prohibits the use of Old Church Slavonic in Great Moravia in favour of Latin
Svatopluk I expels the Byzantine missionaries, and their exiled students take the language to the Bulgarian Empire
The First Bulgarian Empire adopts Old Church Slavonic as its state and liturgical language, and Cyrillic supersedes Glagolitic as official
Kievan Rus’ adopts Orthodox Christianity and with it Old Church Slavonic in the Cyrillic script
The Ostromir Gospel, the earliest manuscript with Russian elements, is written
Patriarch Euthymius of Tarnovo reforms Bulgarian orthography on older Old Church Slavonic models
Mikhail Lomonosov defines three styles for the balance of Church Slavonic and Russian in the literary language

f.family: Slavic; South Slavic branch, Eastern South Slavic subgroup; thought to be based mainly on the 9th-century Slavic dialect of the Byzantine theme of Thessalonica
f.script: Glagolitic, developed for the Moravian mission in 862/863 (about two-thirds of the canon); Cyrillic, developed in the First Bulgarian Empire at the Preslav Literary School and official in Bulgaria from 893
f.earliest: the translations of Cyril and Methodius from 862/863 (the Aprakos Evangeliar, the Psalter, the Acts of the Apostles); the oldest manuscript is usually thought to be the Kiev Missal, of the late 10th century; most manuscripts date from the late 10th and early 11th centuries
f.status: extinct as such; by the mid-11th century it had grown into the regional recensions of Church Slavonic, still the liturgical language of the Bulgarian, Russian, Serbian, Ukrainian and Macedonian Orthodox churches and of several Eastern Catholic churches
